newsitem.title: UK: Authors dish the dirt on Britain's royal family.
newsitem.headline: Authors dish the dirt on Britain's royal family.

text.p: Prince Charles was an adulterer, Princess Diana made serial suicide bids and the Duchess of York betrayed her husband while she was pregnant with Queen Elizabeth's second granddaughter.
These are just some of the revelations in a plethora of books in the past five years, which have focused in much salacious detail on the private lives of Britain's royals.
Among the latest contributions are two books written by former friends of the Duchess of York, or Fergie as she is known, describing in lurid detail her love affairs with two Texan men.
Such exposes are a far cry from the respectful royal biographies to which the British public was accustomed.
Usually written with a royal seal of approval, books about the royals were reverent tomes full of glossy, flattering pictures and paeans to their subject's dignity and compassion.
Those close to the royal family were expected to keep their lips sealed, while newspapers and publishers remained deeply respectful of the monarchy's privacy.

When Edward VIII abdicated in 1936 for the love of an American divorcee, the British public was stunned. While the story of their affair had been widely covered in the foreign press, domestic newspapers had kept a deferential silence.

Marion Crawford, former nanny to the queen and her sister Princess Margaret, suffered swift retribution when she wrote an affectionate book about her royal charges in 1950. "Crawfie" was cut off forever by the royal family.
Royal experts say the climate change surrounding the royals came in 1992 with the publication of "Diana, Her True Story" written by tabloid journalist Andrew Morton.
It portrayed Princess Diana as a tragic figure, spurned by her husband, heir-to-the-throne Prince Charles, and resorting to suicide attempts in her desperate appeals for attention.

It revealed that the glamorous role model Britain believed to be its future queen spent her nights gorging on food and then vomiting it back because she suffered from the eating disorder bulimia nervosa.
Her husband, to the incredulity of the British public, was in love with a dowdy mother of two more than 10 years her senior. The book sold five million copies worldwide.
What was perhaps most astonishing about "Diana, Her True Story" was the fact that the princess had helped the author by encouraging her friends to talk to him about her troubles.
Two years later, Prince Charles put forward his side of their sorry story with a biography written by journalist Jonathan Dimbleby.
Upset by Morton's book portraying him as a cruel, uncaring husband, Charles confessed to adultery, hoping to win approval for his honesty.
But though the public had mixed views about Charles's candour, as far as royal authors were concerned it meant the private lives of the royal family had become fair game.
"Andrew Morton's book was the grand-daddy of them all," said Nigel Evans, editor of Majesty magazine. "Then Charles tried to put the record straight and what followed seemed almost inevitable."
Shortly afterwards, Diana's former lover, cavalry officer James Hewitt, told his story to a romantic novelist who published "Princess in Love," a gushing account of the affair.
Diana's former sister-in-law Fergie is the latest victim of revelations by her former confidants.

In a book published this month, Allan Starkie gives a blow-by-blow account of her affair with one-time "financial adviser" John Bryan who was famously seen sucking her toes in photographs published around the world in 1992.

A clairvoyant who had won Fergie's trust has also published a book about the duchess' extra-marital affairs. She says Fergie began her liaison with Texan Steve Wyatt just three years into her marriage to Prince Andrew, the queen's second son, while she was pregnant with her second daughter.
According to constitutional historian David Starkey, such irreverence towards the royal family is nothing new.
In earlier centuries, the often outrageous behaviour of British royals was public knowledge and they were viciously lampooned by cartoonists.

The monarchy has a long history of unhappy marriages, extramarital affairs and even insanity, from Henry VIII and his serial marriages to Queen Caroline who danced topless at a Geneva ball in the 18th century.
It was only in the Victorian era that the royal family decided to set itself up as a symbol of moral virtue, he said.
"What's happened in the 20th century is really the exception," said Starkey. "What is unusual is the level of adulation and reverence and almost worship that we've seen."
Attitudes towards the monarchy are cyclical, so it was inevitable that the royals should fall from grace, he said. But the behaviour of the young royals has not helped matters.

When the queen's sister Princess Margaret renounced her love for handsome air force officer Peter Townsend in 1955 because he was divorced and therefore considered unsuitable as a royal husband, she was doing what was expected of a princess.
Such self-sacrifice is alien to the younger generation of the royal family. Of the queen's four children, three are divorced and the youngest, Prince Edward, is yet to marry.
